title: Constants and Naming
description: Values that must never change, and the naming conventions every Java programmer follows.

content.value: A Value That Must Not Change

content.real: A rule written in permanent ink
content.text: Some values are decided once: starting lives, a tax rate. `final` locks the value so nothing can overwrite it.

items.title: Normal variable
items.text: A normal variable can change any time.

items.title: final variable
items.text: Compile error: `cannot assign a value to final variable MAX_LIVES`.

content.title: Changing a normal vs a final variable
content.caption: Java catches the mistake before the program ever runs.
A `final` variable is called a **constant**. Give it its value when you declare it.

content.value: `final` does not make the program faster. It states your intention, so a mistake becomes an error instead of a hidden bug.

parts.label: lock
parts.note: The value can never be changed after this.

content.value: Capitals are a convention, not a rule: `final int maxLives = 3;` compiles. But capitals signal "decided once, never changed" to anyone reading.

content.question: Which name follows the convention for a constant?
content.explain: Constants use capitals with underscores between words.

content.value: Why Not Just Write the Number?
A bare number in the middle of your code is a **magic number**: it works, but nothing says what it means.

items.title: Magic numbers
items.text: What are 0.18 and 40 supposed to be?

items.title: Named constants
items.text: Reads like a sentence. Change the rate on one line.

content.title: Magic numbers vs named constants
content.caption: Both give the same total. Only one explains itself.

steps.note: A normal variable: the price could change.
A constant with a name that says what 0.18 is.
500 + 90.0 + 40. One side is a `double`, so the result is 630.0.

content.title: The named version, step by step
content.outro: When the tax rate changes, you edit one line, instead of hunting for every 0.18.

content.caption: Java compiles almost any name. These styles let a reader tell a class from a variable from a constant at a glance.

items.title: Hard to read
items.text: What are n, p and t?

items.title: Reads aloud
items.text: A good name makes a comment unnecessary.

content.title: Names that say what they mean
content.caption: Short names like `i` are fine for a two-line counter (Module 5), and almost nowhere else.

content.question: Which name is written as a class name?
content.explain: Class names use PascalCase: a capital at the start of every word.

practice.question: Declare a constant `PI` holding 3.14159, then use it to print the area of a circle with radius 5. The area is PI times radius times radius.
Try to change a `final` variable and read the error Java gives you. Then comment that line out so the program runs.
Rewrite this program with two named constants so no magic numbers are left, keeping the same answer.

quiz.question: What does `final` do to a variable?
options: Locks its value, so changing it later is a compile error.
Deletes it when the program ends.
quiz.explain: `final` makes the variable a constant. You set the value where you declare it, and Java refuses any later assignment.

quiz.question: How are constant names written by convention?
quiz.explain: Capitals with underscores mark a constant at a glance. Java would compile other styles, but every Java codebase uses this one.

quiz.question: What is a magic number?
options: A bare value in the code with nothing to say what it means.
A number too large for an int.
A number that changes while the program runs.
quiz.explain: A `0.18` sitting in the middle of a calculation tells the reader nothing. Naming it `GST_RATE` explains it and gives you one place to change it.

quiz.question: Which naming style does a class name use?
quiz.explain: Classes start with a capital and capitalise each word. That is why your class is `Main`, not `main`, which is the method.

quiz.question: Why is `double totalCost` better than `double t`?
options: A reader knows what it holds without hunting for an explanation.
Longer names make the program run more accurately.
Java requires names of at least five characters.
quiz.explain: Both compile identically. A good name carries the meaning the code cannot, which matters most when you come back to it weeks later.
